entries.01f28746eabba93aaa2c0f18b3b5817ba65cfefa: <div sID="gen33130" type="x-p"/> <chapter n="12" osisID="Heb.12" sID="Heb.12"/> <div eID="gen33130" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen33131" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen33132" type="x-p"/> The apostle, in this chapter, applies what he has collected in the chapter foregoing, and makes use of it as a great motive to patience and perseverance in the Christian faith and state, pressing home the argument, I. From a greater example than he had yet mentioned, and that is Christ himself, <reference osisRef="Heb.12.1-Heb.12.3">ver. 1-3</reference>. II. From the gentle and gracious nature of the afflictions they endured in their Christian course, <reference osisRef="Heb.12.4-Heb.12.17">ver. 4-17</reference>. III. From the communion and conformity between the state of the gospel-church on earth and the triumphant church in heaven, <reference osisRef="Heb.12.18-Heb.12.29">ver. 18, to the end</reference>.
entries.36904b2cb2599d361f239e76733b68aeaf202b40: <div eID="gen33132" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen33131" type="introduction"/> <title type="x-s3">Christ the Great Exemplar. (<hi type="small-caps">a. d.</hi> 62.)</title> <div sID="gen33133" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">1</hi> Wherefore seeing we also are compassed about with so great a cloud of witnesses, let us lay aside every weight, and the sin which doth so easily beset <hi type="italic">us,</hi> and let us run with patience the race that is set before us, <hi type="super">2</hi> Looking unto Jesus the author and finisher of <hi type="italic">our</hi> faith; who for the joy that was set before him endured the cross, despising the shame, and is set down at the right hand of the throne of God. <hi type="super">3</hi> For consider him that endured such contradiction of sinners against himself, lest ye be wearied and faint in your minds. <div eID="gen33133" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen33134" type="x-p"/> Here observe what is the great duty which the apostle urges upon the Hebrews, and which he so much desires they would comply with, and that is, to <hi type="italic">lay aside every weight, and the sin that did so easily beset them, and run with patience the race set before them.</hi> The duty consists of two parts, the one preparatory, the other perfective. <div eID="gen33134" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen33135" type="x-p"/> I. Preparatory: <hi type="italic">Lay aside every weight, and the sin,</hi> &c. 1. <hi type="italic">Every weight,</hi> that is, all inordinate affection and concern for the body, and the present life and world. Inordinate care for the present life, or fondness for it, is a dead weight upon the soul, that pulls it down when it should ascend upwards, and pulls it back when it should press forward; it makes duty and difficulties harder and heavier than they would be. 2. <hi type="italic">The sin that doth so easily beset us;</hi> the sin that has the greatest advantage against us, by the circumstances we are in, our constitution, our company. This may mean either the damning sin of unbelief or rather the darling sin of the Jews, an over-fondness for their own dispensation. <hi type="italic">Let us lay aside</hi> all external and internal hindrances. <div eID="gen33135" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen33136" type="x-p"/> II. Perfective: <hi type="italic">Run with patience the race that is set before us.</hi> The apostle speaks in the gymnastic style, taken from the Olympic and other exercises. <div eID="gen33136" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen33137" type="x-p"/> 1. Christians have a race to run, a race of service and a race of sufferings, a course of active and passive obedience. <div eID="gen33137" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen33138" type="x-p"/> 2. This race is set before them; it is marked out unto them, both by the word of God and the examples of the faithful servants of God, that cloud of witnesses with which they are compassed about. It is set out by proper limits and directions; the mark they run to, and the prize they run for, are set before them. <div eID="gen33138" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen33139" type="x-p"/> 3. This race must be run with patience and perseverance. There will be need of patience to encounter the difficulties that lie in our way, of perseverance to resist all temptations to desist or turn aside. Faith and patience are the conquering graces, and therefore must be always cultivated and kept in lively exercise. <div eID="gen33139" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen33140" type="x-p"/> 4. Christians have a greater example to animate and encourage them in their Christian course than any or all who have been mentioned before, and that is the Lord Jesus Christ: <hi type="italic">Looking unto Jesus, the author and finisher of our faith,</hi> <reference osisRef="Heb.12.2">v. 2</reference>. Here observe, <div eID="gen33140" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen33141" type="x-p"/> (1.) What our Lord Jesus is to his people: he is <hi type="italic">the author and finisher of</hi> their <hi type="italic">faith</hi>—the beginning, perfecter, and rewarder of it. [1.] He is the author of their faith; not only the object, but the author. He is the great leader and precedent of our faith, <hi type="italic">he trusted in God;</hi> he is the purchaser of the Spirit of faith, the publisher of the rule of faith, the efficient cause of the grace of faith, and in all respects the author of our faith. [2.] He is <hi type="italic">the finisher of our faith;</hi> he is the fulfiller and the fulfilling of all scripture-promises and prophecies; he is the perfecter of the canon of scripture; he is the finisher of grace, and of the work of faith with power in the souls of his people; and he is the judge and the rewarder of their faith; he determines who they are that reach the mark, and from him, and in him, they have the prize. <div eID="gen33141" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen33142" type="x-p"/> (2.) What trials Christ met with in his race and course. [1.] He <hi type="italic">endured the contradiction of sinners against himself</hi> (<reference osisRef="Heb.12.3">v. 3</reference>); he bore the opposition that they made to him, both in their words and behaviour. They were continually contradicting him, and crossing in upon his great designs; and though he could easily have both confuted and confounded them, and sometimes gave them a specimen of his power, yet he endured their evil manners with great patience. Their contradictions were levelled against Christ himself, against his person as God-man, against his authority, against his preaching, and yet he endured all. [2.] He <hi type="italic">endured the cross</hi>—all those sufferings that he met with in the world; for he took up his cross betimes, and was at length nailed to it, and endured a painful, ignominious, and accursed death, in which he was numbered with the transgressors, the vilest malefactors; yet all this he endured with invincible patience and resolution. [3.] He <hi type="italic">despised the shame.</hi> All the reproaches that were cast upon him, both in his life and at his death, he despised; he was infinitely above them; he knew his own innocency and excellency, and despised the ignorance and malice of his despisers. <div eID="gen33142" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen33143" type="x-p"/> (3.) What it was that supported the human soul of Christ under these unparalleled sufferings; and that was <hi type="italic">the joy that was set before him.</hi> He had something in view under all his sufferings, which was pleasant to him; he rejoiced to see that by his sufferings he should make satisfaction to the injured justice of God and give security to his honour and government, that he should make peace between God and man, that he should seal the covenant of grace and be the Mediator of it, that he should open a way of salvation to the chief of sinners, and that he should effectually save all those whom the Father had given him, and himself be the first-born among many brethren. This was the joy that was set before him. <div eID="gen33143" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen33144" type="x-p"/> (4.) The reward of his suffering: he <hi type="italic">has sat down at the right hand of the throne of God.</hi> Christ, as Mediator, is exalted to a station of the highest honour, of the greatest power and influence; he is at the right hand of the Father. Nothing passes between heaven and earth but by him; he does all that is done; <hi type="italic">he ever lives to make intercession for</hi> his people. <div eID="gen33144" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen33145" type="x-p"/> (5.) What is our duty with respect to this Jesus. We must, [1.] Look unto him; that is, we must set him continually before us as our example, and our great encouragement; we must look to him for direction, for assistance, and for acceptance, in all our sufferings. [2.] We must consider him, meditate much upon him, and reason with ourselves from his case to our own. We must <hi type="italic">analogize,</hi> as the word is; compare Christ's sufferings and ours; and we shall find that as his sufferings far exceeded ours, in the nature and measure of them, so his patience far excels ours, and is a perfect pattern for us to imitate. <div eID="gen33145" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen33146" type="x-p"/> (6.) The advantage we shall reap by thus doing: it will be a means to prevent our weariness and fainting (<reference osisRef="Heb.12.3">v. 3</reference>): <hi type="italic">Lest you be weary and faint in your minds.</hi> Observe, [1.] There is a proneness in the best to grow weary and to faint under their trials and afflictions, especially when they prove heavy and of long continuance: this proceeds from the imperfections of grace and the remains of corruption. [2.] The best way to prevent this is to look unto Jesus, and to consider him. Faith and meditation will fetch in fresh supplies of strength, comfort, and courage; for he has assured them, if <hi type="italic">they suffer with him, they shall also reign with him:</hi> and this hope will be their helmet.
entries.ee787410bbabb8bac885c3d6cc8d74fddc082494: <div eID="gen33146" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s3">The Benefit of Afflictions; The Use of Afflictions; Cautions against Apostasy. (<hi type="small-caps">a. d.</hi> 62.)</title> <div sID="gen33147" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">4</hi> Ye have not yet resisted unto blood, striving against sin. <hi type="super">5</hi> And ye have forgotten the exhortation which speaketh unto you as unto children, My son, despise not thou the chastening of the Lord, nor faint when thou art rebuked of him: 6 For whom the Lord loveth he chasteneth, and scourgeth every son whom he receiveth. <hi type="super">7</hi> If ye endure chastening, God dealeth with you as with sons; for what son is he whom the father chasteneth not? <hi type="super">8</hi> But if ye be without chastisement, whereof all are partakers, then are ye bastards, and not sons. <hi type="super">9</hi> Furthermore we have had fathers of our flesh which corrected <hi type="italic">us,</hi> and we gave <hi type="italic">them</hi> reverence: shall we not much rather be in subjection unto the Father of spirits, and live? 10 For they verily for a few days chastened <hi type="italic">us</hi> after their own pleasure; but he for <hi type="italic">our</hi> profit, that <hi type="italic">we</hi> might be partakers of his holiness. <hi type="super">11</hi> Now no chastening for the present seemeth to be joyous, but grievous: nevertheless afterward it yieldeth the peaceable fruit of righteousness unto them which are exercised thereby. <hi type="super">12</hi> Wherefore lift up the hands which hang down, and the feeble knees; <hi type="super">13</hi> And make straight paths for your feet, lest that which is lame be turned out of the way; but let it rather be healed. <hi type="super">14</hi> Follow peace with all <hi type="italic">men,</hi> and holiness, without which no man shall see the Lord: <hi type="super">15</hi> Looking diligently lest any man fail of the grace of God; lest any root of bitterness springing up trouble <hi type="italic">you,</hi> and thereby many be defiled; <hi type="super">16</hi> Lest there <hi type="italic">be</hi> any fornicator, or profane person, as Esau, who for one morsel of meat sold his birthright. <hi type="super">17</hi> For ye know how that afterward, when he would have inherited the blessing, he was rejected: for he found no place of repentance, though he sought it carefully with tears. <div eID="gen33147" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen33148" type="x-p"/> Here the apostle presses the exhortation to patience and perseverance by an argument taken from the gentle measure and gracious nature of those sufferings which the believing Hebrews endured in their Christian course. <div eID="gen33148" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen33149" type="x-p"/> I. From the gentle and moderate degree and measure of their sufferings: <hi type="italic">You have not yet resisted unto blood, striving against sin,</hi> <reference osisRef="Heb.12.4">v. 4</reference>. Observe, <div eID="gen33149" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen33150" type="x-p"/> 1. He owns that they had suffered much, they had been striving to an agony against sin. Here, (1.) The cause of the conflict was sin, and to be engaged against sin is to fight in a good cause, for sin is the worst enemy both to God and man. Our spiritual warfare is both honourable and necessary; for we are only defending ourselves against that which would destroy us, if it should get the victory over us; we fight for ourselves, for our lives, and therefore ought to be patient and resolute. (2.) Every Christian is enlisted under Christ's banner, to strive against sin, against sinful doctrines, sinful practices, and sinful habits and customs, both in himself and in others. <div eID="gen33150" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen33151" type="x-p"/> 2. He puts them in mind that they might have suffered more, that they had not suffered as much as others; for they had <hi type="italic">not yet resisted unto blood,</hi> they had not been called to martyrdom as yet, though they knew not how soon they might be. Learn here, (1.) Our Lord Jesus, <hi type="italic">the captain of our salvation,</hi> does not call his people out to the hardest trials at first, but wisely trains them up by less sufferings to be prepared for greater. He will not put new wine into weak vessels, he is <hi type="italic">the gentle shepherd,</hi> who will not overdrive <hi type="italic">the young ones of the flock.</hi> (2.) It becomes Christians to take notice of the gentleness of Christ in accommodating their trial to their strength. They should not magnify their afflictions, but should take notice of the mercy that is mixed with them, and should pity those who are called to the fiery trials to <hi type="italic">resist to blood;</hi> not to shed the blood of their enemies, but to seal their testimony with their own blood. (3.) Christians should be ashamed to faint under less trials, when they see others bear up under greater, and do not know how soon they may meet with greater themselves. If we have run with the footmen and they have wearied us, how shall we contend with horses? If we be wearied in a land of peace, what shall we do in the swellings of Jordan? <reference osisRef="Jer.12.5">Jer. xii. 5</reference>. <div eID="gen33151" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen33152" type="x-p"/> II. He argues from the peculiar and gracious nature of those sufferings that befall the people of God. Though their enemies and persecutors may be the instruments of inflicting such sufferings on them, yet they are divine chastisements; their heavenly Father has his hand in all, and his wise end to serve by all; of this he has given them due notice, and they should not forget it, <reference osisRef="Heb.12.5">v. 5</reference>. Observe, <div eID="gen33152" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen33153" type="x-p"/> 1. Those afflictions which may be truly persecution as far as men are concerned in them are fatherly rebukes and chastisements as far as God is concerned in them. Persecution for religion is sometimes a correction and rebuke for the sins of professors of religion. Men persecute them because they are religious; God chastises them because they are not more so: men persecute them because they will not give up their profession; God chastises them because they have not lived up to their profession. <div eID="gen33153" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen33154" type="x-p"/> 2. God has directed his people how they ought to behave themselves under all their afflictions; they must avoid the extremes that many run into. (1.) They must not despise the chastening of the Lord; they must not make light of afflictions, and be stupid and insensible under them, for they are the hand and rod of God, and his rebukes for sin. Those who make light of affliction make light of God and make light of sin. (2.) They must not faint when they are rebuked; they must not despond and sink under their trial, nor fret and repine, but bear up with faith and patience. (3.) If they run into either of these extremes, it is a sign they have forgotten their heavenly Father's advice and exhortation, which he has given them in true and tender affection. <div eID="gen33154" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen33155" type="x-p"/> 3. Afflictions, rightly endured, though they may be the fruits of God's displeasure, are yet proofs of his paternal love to his people and care for them (<reference osisRef="Heb.12.6-Heb.12.7">v. 6, 7</reference>): <hi type="italic">Whom the Lord loveth he chasteneth, and scourgeth every son whom he receiveth.</hi> Observe, (1.) The best of God's children need chastisement. They have their faults and follies, which need to be corrected. (2.) Though God may let others alone in their sins, he will correct sin in his own children; they are of his family, and shall not escape his rebukes when they want them. (3.) In this he acts as becomes a father, and treats them like children; no wise and good father will wink at faults in his own children as he would in others; his relation and his affections oblige him to take more notice of the faults of his own children than those of others. (4.) To be suffered to go on in sin without a rebuke is a sad sign of alienation from God; such are bastards, not sons. They may call him Father, because born in the pale of the church; but they are the spurious offspring of another father, not of God, <reference osisRef="Heb.12.7-Heb.12.8">v. 7, 8</reference>. <div eID="gen33155" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen33156" type="x-p"/> 4. Those that are impatient under the discipline of their heavenly Father behave worse towards him than they would do towards earthly parents, <reference osisRef="Heb.12.9-Heb.12.10">v. 9, 10</reference>. Here, (1.) The apostle commends a dutiful and submissive behaviour in children towards their earthly parents <hi type="italic">We gave them reverence,</hi> even when they corrected us. It is the duty of children to give the reverence of obedience to the just commands of their parents, and the reverence of submission to their correction when they have been disobedient. Parents have not only authority, but a charge from God, to give their children correction when it is due, and he has commanded children to take such correction well: to be stubborn and discontented under due correction is a double fault; for the correction supposes there has been a fault already committed against the parent's commanding power, and superadds a further fault against his chastening power. Hence, (2.) He recommends humble and submissive behavior towards our heavenly Father, when under his correction; and this he does by an argument from the less to the greater. [1.] Our earthly fathers are but <hi type="italic">the fathers of our flesh,</hi> but God is <hi type="italic">the Father of our spirits.</hi> Our fathers on earth were instrumental in the production of our bodies, which are but flesh, a mean, mortal, vile thing, formed out of the dust of the earth, as the bodies of the beasts are; and yet as they are curiously wrought, and made parts of our persons, a proper tabernacle for the soul to dwell in and an organ for it to act by, we owe reverence and affection to those who were instrumental in their procreation; but then we must own much more to him who is the Father of our spirits. Our souls are not of a material substance, not of the most refined sort; they are not <hi type="italic">ex traduce—by traduction;</hi> to affirm it is bad philosophy, and worse divinity: they are the immediate offspring of God, who, after he had formed the body of man out of the earth, breathed into him a vital spirit, and so he became a living soul. [2.] Our earthly parents <hi type="italic">chastened us for their own pleasure.</hi> Sometimes they did it to gratify their passion rather than to reform our manners. This is a weakness the fathers of our flesh are subject to, and this they should carefully watch against; for hereby they dishonour that parental authority which God has put upon them and very much hinder the efficacy of their chastisements. But the Father of our spirits never grieves willingly, nor afflicts the children of men, much less his own children. It is always <hi type="italic">for our profit;</hi> and the advantage he intends us thereby is no less than our being partakers of his holiness; it is to correct and cure those sinful disorders which make us unlike to God, and to improve and to increase those graces which are the image of God in us, that we may be and act more like our heavenly Father. God loves his children so that he would have them to be as like himself as can be, and for this end he chastises them when they need it. [3.] The fathers of our flesh corrected us for <hi type="italic">a few days,</hi> in our state of childhood, when minors; and, though we were in that weak and peevish state, we owed them reverence, and when we came to maturity we loved and honoured them the more for it. Our whole life here is a state of childhood, minority, and imperfection, and therefore we must submit to the discipline of such a state; when we come to a state of perfection we shall be fully reconciled to all the measures of God's discipline over us now. [4.] God's correction is no condemnation. His children may at first fear lest affliction should come upon that dreadful errand, and we cry, <hi type="italic">Do not condemn me,</hi> but <hi type="italic">show me wherefore thou contendest with me,</hi> <reference osisRef="Job.10.2">Job x. 2</reference>. But this is so far from being the design of God to his own people that he therefore chastens them now <hi type="italic">that they may not be condemned with the world,</hi> <reference osisRef="1Cor.11.32">1 Cor. xi. 32</reference>. He does it to prevent the death and destruction of their souls, that they may live to God, and be like God, and for ever with him. <div eID="gen33156" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen33157" type="x-p"/> 5. The children of God, under their afflictions, ought not to judge of his dealings with them by present sense, but by reason, and faith, and experience: <hi type="italic">No chastening for the present seemeth to be joyous, but grievous; nevertheless afterwards it yieldeth the peaceable fruits of righteousness,</hi> <reference osisRef="Heb.12.11">v. 11</reference>. Here observe, <div eID="gen33157" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen33158" type="x-p"/> (1.) The judgment of sense in this case—Afflictions are not grateful to the sense, but grievous; the flesh will feel them, and be grieved by them, and groan under them. <div eID="gen33158" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen33159" type="x-p"/> (2.) The judgment of faith, which corrects that of sense, and declares that a sanctified affliction produces the fruits of righteousness; these fruits are peaceable, and tend to the quieting and comforting of the soul. Affliction produces peace, by producing more righteousness; for the fruit of righteousness is peace. And if the pain of the body contribute thus to the peace of the mind, and short present affliction produce blessed fruits of a long continuance, they have no reason to fret or faint under it; but their great concern is that the chastening they are under may be endured by them with patience, and improved to a greater degree of holiness. [1.] That their affliction may be endured with patience, which is the main drift of the apostle's discourse on this subject; and he again returns to exhort them that for the reason before mentioned they should <hi type="italic">lift up the hands that hang down and the feeble knees,</hi> <reference osisRef="Heb.12.12">v. 12</reference>. A burden of affliction is apt to make the Christian's hands hang down, and his knees grow feeble, to dispirit him and discourage him; but this he must strive against, and that for two reasons:—<hi type="italic">First,</hi> That he may the better run his spiritual race and course. Faith, and patience, and holy courage and resolution, will make him walk more steadily, keep a straighter path, prevent wavering and wandering. <hi type="italic">Secondly,</hi> That he may encourage and not dispirit others that are in the same way with him. There are many that are in the way to heaven who yet walk but weakly and lamely in it. Such are apt to discourage one another, and hinder one another; but it is their duty to take courage, and act by faith, and so help one another forward in the way to heaven. [2.] That their affliction may be improved to a greater degree of holiness. Since this is God's design, it ought to be the design and concern of his children, that with renewed strength and patience they may <hi type="italic">follow peace with all men, and holiness,</hi> <reference osisRef="Heb.12.14">v. 14</reference>. If the children of God grow impatient under affliction, they will neither walk so quietly and peaceably towards men, nor so piously towards God, as they should do; but faith and patience will enable them to follow peace and holiness too, as a man follows his calling, constantly, diligently, and with pleasure. Observe, <hi type="italic">First,</hi> It is the duty of Christians, even when in a suffering state, <hi type="italic">to follow peace with all men,</hi> yea, even with those who may be instrumental in their sufferings. This is a hard lesson, and a high attainment, but it is what Christ has called his people to. Sufferings are apt to sour the spirit and sharpen the passions; but the children of God must follow peace with all men. <hi type="italic">Secondly,</hi> Peace and holiness are connected together; there can be no true peace without holiness. There may be prudence and discreet forbearance, and a show of friendship and good-will to all; but this true Christian peaceableness is never found separate from holiness. We must not, under pretence of living peaceably with all men, leave the ways of holiness, but cultivate peace in a way of holiness. <hi type="italic">Thirdly, Without holiness no man shall see the Lord.</hi> The vision of God our Saviour in heaven is reserved as the reward of holiness, and the stress of our salvation is laid upon our holiness, though a placid peaceable disposition contributes much to our meetness for heaven. <div eID="gen33159" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen33160" type="x-p"/> 6. Where afflictions and sufferings for the sake of Christ are not considered by men as the chastisement of their heavenly Father, and improved as such, they will be a dangerous snare and temptation to apostasy, which every Christian should most carefully watch against (<reference osisRef="Heb.12.15-Heb.12.16">v. 15, 16</reference>): <hi type="italic">Looking diligently lest any man fail of the grace of God,</hi> &c. <div eID="gen33160" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen33161" type="x-p"/> (1.) Here the apostle enters a serious caveat against apostasy, and backs it with an awful example. <div eID="gen33161" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen33162" type="x-p"/> [1.] He enters a serious caveat against apostasy, <reference osisRef="Heb.12.15">v. 15</reference>. Here you may observe, <hi type="italic">First,</hi> The nature of apostasy: it is <hi type="italic">failing of the grace of God;</hi> it is to become bankrupts in religion, for want of a good foundation, and suitable care and diligence; it is <hi type="italic">failing of the grace of God,</hi> coming short of a principle of true grace in the soul, notwithstanding the means of grace and a profession of religion, and so coming short of the love and favour of God here and hereafter. <hi type="italic">Secondly,</hi> The consequences of apostasy: where persons fail of having the true grace of God, a root of bitterness will spring up, corruption will prevail and break forth. A <hi type="italic">root of bitterness,</hi> a bitter root, producing bitter fruits to themselves and others. It produces to themselves corrupt principles, which lead to apostasy and are greatly strengthened and radicated by apostasy—damnable errors (to the corrupting of the doctrine and worship of the Christian church) and corrupt practices. Apostates generally grow worse and worse, and fall into the grossest wickedness, which usually ends either in downright atheism or in despair. It also produces bitter fruits to others, to the churches to which these men belonged; by their corrupt principles and practices many are troubled, the peace of the church is broken, the peace of men's minds is disturbed, and <hi type="italic">many are defiled,</hi> tainted with those bad principles, and drawn into defiling practices; so that the churches suffer both in their purity and peace. But the apostates themselves will be the greatest sufferers at last. <div eID="gen33162" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen33163" type="x-p"/> [2.] The apostle backs the caution with an awful example, and that is, that of Esau, who though born within the pale of the church, and having the birthright as the eldest son, and so entitled to the privilege of being prophet, priest, and king, in his family, was so profane as to despise these sacred privileges, and to sell his birthright for a morsel of meat. Where observe, <hi type="italic">First,</hi> Esau's sin. He profanely despised and sold the birthright, and all the advantages attending it. So do apostates, who to avoid persecution, and enjoy sensual ease and pleasure, though they bore the character of the children of God, and had a visible right to the blessing and inheritance, give up all pretensions thereto. <hi type="italic">Secondly,</hi> Esau's punishment, which was suitable to his sin. His conscience was convinced of his sin and folly, when it was too late: <hi type="italic">He would afterwards have inherited the blessing,</hi> &c. His punishment lay in two things: 1. He was condemned by his own conscience; he now saw that the blessing he had made so light of was worth the having, worth the seeking, though with much carefulness and many tears. 2. He was rejected of God: <hi type="italic">He found no place of repentance</hi> in God or in his father; the blessing was given to another, even to him to whom he sold it for a mess of pottage. Esau, in his great wickedness, had made the bargain, and God in his righteous judgment, ratified and confirmed it, and would not suffer Isaac to reverse it. <div eID="gen33163" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen33164" type="x-p"/> (2.) We may hence learn, [1.] That apostasy from Christ is the fruit of preferring the gratification of the flesh to the blessing of God and the heavenly inheritance. [2.] Sinners will not always have such mean thoughts of the divine blessing and inheritance as now they have. The time is coming when they will think no pains too great, no cares no tears too much, to obtain the lost blessing. [3.] When the day of grace is over (as sometimes it may be in this life), they will find no place for repentance: they cannot repent aright of their sin; and God will not repent of the sentence he has passed upon them for their sin. And therefore, as the design of all, Christians should never give up their title, and hope of their Father's blessing and inheritance, and expose themselves to his irrevocable wrath and curse, by deserting their holy religion, to avoid suffering, which, though this may be persecution as far as wicked men are concerned in it, is only a rod of correction and chastisement in the hand of their heavenly Father, to bring them near to himself in conformity and communion. This is the force of the apostle's arguing from the nature of the sufferings of the people of God even when they suffer for righteousness' sake; and the reasoning is very strong.
entries.f11edd80cf8c8defe3014ea266adaa2ce3c3bc6f: <div eID="gen33164" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s3">Nature of the Christian Economy. (<hi type="small-caps">a. d.</hi> 62.)</title> <div sID="gen33165" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">18</hi> For ye are not come unto the mount that might be touched, and that burned with fire, nor unto blackness, and darkness, and tempest, <hi type="super">19</hi> And the sound of a trumpet, and the voice of words; which <hi type="italic">voice</hi> they that heard intreated that the word should not be spoken to them any more: <hi type="super">20</hi> (For they could not endure that which was commanded, And if so much as a beast touch the mountain, it shall be stoned, or thrust through with a dart: <hi type="super">21</hi> And so terrible was the sight, <hi type="italic">that</hi> Moses said, I exceedingly fear and quake:) <hi type="super">22</hi> But ye are come unto mount Sion, and unto the city of the living God, the heavenly Jerusalem, and to an innumerable company of angels, <hi type="super">23</hi> To the general assembly and church of the firstborn, which are written in heaven, and to God the Judge of all, and to the spirits of just men made perfect, <hi type="super">24</hi> And to Jesus the mediator of the new covenant, and to the blood of sprinkling, that speaketh better things than <hi type="italic">that of</hi> Abel. <hi type="super">25</hi> See that ye refuse not him that speaketh. For if they escaped not who refused him that spake on earth, much more <hi type="italic">shall not</hi> we <hi type="italic">escape,</hi> if we turn away from him that <hi type="italic">speaketh</hi> from heaven: <hi type="super">26</hi> Whose voice then shook the earth: but now he hath promised, saying, Yet once more I shake not the earth only, but also heaven. <hi type="super">27</hi> And this <hi type="italic">word,</hi> Yet once more, signifieth the removing of those things that are shaken, as of things that are made, that those things which cannot be shaken may remain. <hi type="super">28</hi> Wherefore we receiving a kingdom which cannot be moved, let us have grace, whereby we may serve God acceptably with reverence and godly fear: <hi type="super">29</hi> For our God <hi type="italic">is</hi> a consuming fire. <div eID="gen33165" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen33166" type="x-p"/> Here the apostle goes on to engage the professing Hebrews to perseverance in their Christian course and conflict, and not to relapse again into Judaism. This he does by showing them how much the state of the gospel church differs from that of the Jewish church, and how much it resembles the state of the church in heaven, and on both accounts demands and deserves our diligence, patience, and perseverance in Christianity. <div eID="gen33166" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen33167" type="x-p"/> I. He shows how much the gospel church differs from the Jewish church, and how much it excels. And here we have a very particular description of the state of the church under the Mosaic dispensation, <reference osisRef="Heb.12.18-Heb.12.21">v. 18-21</reference>. 1. It was a gross sensible state. Mount Sinai, on which that church-state was constituted, was a <hi type="italic">mount that might be touched</hi> (<reference osisRef="Heb.12.18">v. 18</reference>), a gross palpable place; so was the dispensation. It was very much external and earthly, and so more heavy. The state of the gospel church on mount Zion is more spiritual, rational, and easy. 2. It was a dark dispensation. Upon that mount there were blackness and darkness, and that church-state was covered with dark shadows and types: the gospel state is much more clear and bright. 3. It was a dreadful and terrible dispensation; the Jews could not bear the terror of it. The thunder and the lightning, the trumpet sounding, the voice of God himself speaking to them, struck them with such dread that they <hi type="italic">entreated that the word might not be so spoken to them any more,</hi> <reference osisRef="Heb.12.19">v. 19</reference>. Yea, Moses himself said, <hi type="italic">I exceedingly fear and quake.</hi> The best of men on earth are not able to converse immediately with God and his holy angels. The gospel state is mild, and kind, and condescending, suited to our weak frame. 4. It was a limited dispensation; all might not approach to that mount, but only Moses and Aaron. Under the gospel we have all access with boldness to God. 5. It was a very dangerous dispensation. The mount burned with fire, and whatever man or beast touched the mount must <hi type="italic">be stoned, or thrust through with a dart,</hi> <reference osisRef="Heb.12.20">v. 20</reference>. It is true, it will be always dangerous for presumptuous and brutish sinners to draw nigh to God; but it is not immediate and certain death, as here it was. This was the state of the Jewish church, fitted to awe a stubborn and hard-hearted people, to set forth the strict and tremendous justice of God, to wean the people of God from that dispensation, and induce them more readily to embrace the sweet and gentle economy of the gospel church, and adhere to it. <div eID="gen33167" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen33168" type="x-p"/> II. He shows how much the gospel church represents the church triumphant in heaven, what communication there is between the one and the other. The gospel church is called <hi type="italic">mount Zion, the heavenly Jerusalem, which is free,</hi> in opposition to mount Sinai, which tendeth to bondage, <reference osisRef="Gal.4.24">Gal. iv. 24</reference>. This was the hill on which God set his king the Messiah. Now, in coming to mount Zion, believers come into heavenly places, and into a heavenly society. <div eID="gen33168" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen33169" type="x-p"/> 1. Into heavenly places. (1.) <hi type="italic">Unto the city of the living God.</hi> God has taken up his gracious residence in the gospel church, which on that account is an emblem of heaven. There his people may find him ruling, guiding, sanctifying, and comforting them; there he speaks to them by the gospel ministry; there they speak to him by prayer, and he hears them; there he trains them up for heaven, and gives them the earnest of their inheritance. (2.) To <hi type="italic">the heavenly Jerusalem</hi> as born and bred there, as free denizens there. Here believers have clearer views of heaven, plainer evidences for heaven, and a greater meetness and more heavenly temper of soul. <div eID="gen33169" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen33170" type="x-p"/> 2. To a heavenly society. (1.) <hi type="italic">To an innumerable company of angels,</hi> who are of the same family with the saints, under the same head, and in a great measure employed in the same work, ministering to believers for their good, keeping them in all their ways, and pitching their tents about them. These for number are innumerable, and for order and union are a company, and a glorious one. And those who by faith are joined to the gospel church are joined to the angels, and shall at length be like them, and equal with them. (2.) <hi type="italic">To the general assembly and church of the first-born, that are written in heaven,</hi> that is, to the universal church, however dispersed. By faith we come to them, have communion with them in the same head, by the same Spirit, and in the same blessed hope, and walk in the same way of holiness, grappling with the same spiritual enemies, and hasting to the same rest, victory, and glorious triumph. Here will be the general assembly of the first-born, the saints of former and earlier times, who saw the promises of the gospel state, but received them not, as well as those who first received them under the gospel, and were regenerated thereby, and so were the first-born, and the first-fruits of the gospel church; and thereby, as the first-born, advanced to greater honours and privileges than the rest of the world. Indeed all the children of God are heirs, and every one has the privileges of the first-born. The names of these are written in heaven, in the records of the church here: they have a name in God's house, are written among the living in Jerusalem; they have a good repute for their faith and fidelity, and are enrolled in the Lamb's book of life, as citizens are enrolled in the livery-books. (3.) <hi type="italic">To God the Judge of all,</hi> that great God who will judge both Jew and Gentile according to the law they are under: believers come to him now by faith, make supplication to their Judge, and receive a sentence of absolution in the gospel, and in the court of their consciences now, by which they know they shall be justified hereafter. (4.) <hi type="italic">To the spirits of just men made perfect;</hi> to the best sort of men, the righteous, who are more excellent than their neighbours; to the best part of just men, their spirits, and to these in their best state, made perfect. Believers have union with departed saints in one and the same head and Spirit, and a title to the same inheritance, of which those on earth are heirs, those in heaven possessors. (5.) <hi type="italic">To Jesus the Mediator of the new covenant, and to the blood of sprinkling, that speaketh better things than that of Abel.</hi> This is none of the least of many encouragements there are to perseverance in the gospel state, since it is a state of communion with Christ the Mediator of the new covenant, and of communication of his blood, that speaketh better things than the blood of Abel. [1.] The gospel covenant is the new covenant, distinct from the covenant of works; and it is now under a new dispensation, distinct from that of the Old Testament. [2.] Christ is the Mediator of this new covenant; he is the middle person that goes between both parties, God and man, to bring them together in this covenant, to keep them together notwithstanding the sins of the people and God's displeasure against them for sin, to offer up our prayers to God, and to bring down the favours of God to us, to plead with God for us and to plead with us for God, and at length to bring God and his people together in heaven, and to be a Mediator of fruition between them for ever, they beholding and enjoying God in Christ and God beholding and blessing them in Christ. [3.] This covenant is ratified by the blood of Christ sprinkled upon our consciences, as the blood of the sacrifice was sprinkled upon the altar and the sacrifice. This blood of Christ pacifies God and purifies the consciences of men. [4.] This is speaking blood, and it speaks better things than that of Abel. <hi type="italic">First,</hi> It speaks to God in behalf of sinners; it pleads not for vengeance, as the blood of Abel did on him who shed it, but for mercy. <hi type="italic">Secondly,</hi> To sinners, in the name of God. It speaks pardon to their sins, peace to their souls; and bespeaks their strictest obedience and highest love and thankfulness. <div eID="gen33170" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen33171" type="x-p"/> III. The apostle, having thus enlarged upon the argument to perseverance taken from the heavenly nature of the gospel church state, closes the chapter by improving the argument in a manner suitable to the weight of it (<reference osisRef="Heb.12.25">v. 25</reference>, &c.): <hi type="italic">See then that you refuse not him that speaketh</hi>—that speaketh by his blood; and not only speaketh after another manner than the blood of Abel spoke from the ground, but than God spoke by the angels, and by Moses spoke on mount Sinai; then he spoke on earth, now he speaks from heaven. Here observe, <div eID="gen33171" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen33172" type="x-p"/> 1. When God speaks to men in the most excellent manner he justly expects from them the most strict attention and regard. Now it is in the gospel that God speaks to men in the most excellent manner. For, (1.) He now speaks from a higher and more glorious seat and throne, not from mount Sinai, which was on this earth, but from heaven. (2.) He speaks now more immediately by his inspired word and by his Spirit, which are his witnesses. He speaks not now any new thing to men, but by his Spirit speaks the same word home to the conscience. (3.) He speaks now more powerfully and effectually. Then indeed his voice shook the earth, but now, by introducing the gospel state, he hath shaken not only the earth, but the heavens,—not only shaken the hills and mountains, or the spirits of men, or the civil state of the land of Canaan, to make room for his people,—not only shaken the world, as he then did, but he hath shaken the church, that is, the Jewish nation, and shaken them in their church-state, which was in Old-Testament times a heaven upon earth; this their heavenly spiritual state he hath now shaken. It is by the gospel from heaven that God shook to pieces the civil and ecclesiastical state of the Jewish nation, and introduced a new state of the church, that cannot be removed, shall never be changed for any other on earth, but shall remain till it be made perfect in heaven. <div eID="gen33172" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen33173" type="x-p"/> 2. When God speaks to men in the most excellent manner, the guilt of those who refuse him is the greater, and their punishment will be more unavoidable and intolerable; there is no escaping, no bearing it, <reference osisRef="Heb.12.25">v. 25</reference>. The different manner of God's dealing with men under the gospel, in a way of grace, assures us that he will deal with the despisers of the gospel after a different manner than he does with other men, in a way of judgment. The glory of the gospel, which should greatly recommend it to our regard, appears in these three things:—(1.) It was by the sound of the gospel trumpet that the former dispensation and state of the church of God were shaken and removed; and shall we despise that voice of God that pulled down a church and state of so long standing and of God's own building? (2.) It was by the sound of the gospel trumpet that a new kingdom was erected for God in the world, which can never be so shaken as to be removed. This was a change made once for all; no other change shall take place <hi type="italic">till time shall be no more.</hi> We have now <hi type="italic">received a kingdom that cannot be moved,</hi> shall never be removed, never give way to any new dispensation. The canon of scripture is now perfected, <hi type="italic">the Spirit of prophecy has ceased,</hi> the mystery of God is finished, he has put his last hand to it. The gospel church may be made more large, more prosperous more purified from contracted pollution, but it shall never be altered for another dispensation; those who perish under the gospel perish without remedy. And hence the apostle justly concludes, [1.] How necessary it is for us to obtain <hi type="italic">grace from God, to serve him acceptably:</hi> if we be not accepted of God under this dispensation, we shall never be accepted at all; and we lose all our labour in religion if we be not accepted of God. [2.] We cannot worship God acceptably, unless we worship him with <hi type="italic">godly reverence and fear.</hi> As faith, so holy fear, is necessary to acceptable worship. [3.] It is only the grace of God that enables us to worship God in a right manner: nature cannot come up to it; it can produce neither that precious faith nor that holy fear that is necessary to acceptable worship. [4.] God is the same just and righteous God under the gospel that he appeared to be under the law. Though he be our God in Christ, and now deals with us in a more kind and gracious way, yet he is in himself a consuming fire; that is, a God of strict justice, who will avenge himself on all the despisers of his grace, and upon all apostates. Under the gospel, the justice of God is displayed in a more awful manner, though not in so sensible a manner as under the law; for here we behold divine justice seizing upon the Lord Jesus Christ, and making him a propitiatory sacrifice, his soul and body an offering for sin, which is a display of justice far beyond what was seen and heard on mount Sinai when the law was given.  <chapter eID="Heb.12"/> <div eID="gen33173" type="x-p"/>

entries.c5e90338aaff9dcd369297428ba4b8767c1460f2: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv18566"/><title type="x-s2">CHAPTER 12</title> <title type="x-s3"><reference osisRef="Heb.12.1-Heb.12.29">He 12:1-29</reference>. Exhortation to Follow the Witnesses of Faith Just Mentioned: Not to Faint in Trials: To Remove All Bitter Roots of Sin:</title> <div sID="gen39153" type="x-p"/> For We Are under, Not a Law of Terror, but the Gospel of Grace, to Despise Which Will Bring the Heavier Penalties, in Proportion to Our Greater Privileges.<div eID="gen39153" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen39154" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv18566"/><hi type="bold">1. we also--</hi>as well as those recounted in <reference osisRef="Heb.12.11">He 12:11</reference>.<div eID="gen39154" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen39155" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">are compassed about--</hi>Greek, "have so great a cloud (a numberless multitude above us, like a cloud, 'holy and pellucid,' [Clement of Alexandria]) of witnesses surrounding us." The image is from a "race," an image common even in Palestine from the time of the Greco-Macedonian empire, which introduced such Greek usages as national games. The "witnesses" answer to the spectators pressing round to see the competitors in their contest for the prize (<reference osisRef="Phil.3.14">Php 3:14</reference>). Those "witnessed of" (Greek, <reference osisRef="Heb.11.5">He 11:5</reference>, <reference osisRef="Heb.11.39">39</reference>) become in their turn "witnesses" in a twofold way: (1) attesting by their own case the faithfulness of God to His people [Alford] (<reference osisRef="Heb.6.12">He 6:12</reference>), some of them martyrs in the modern sense; (2) witnessing our struggle of faith; however, this second sense of "witnesses," though agreeing with the image here if it is to be pressed, is not positively, unequivocally, and directly sustained by Scripture. It gives vividness to the image; as the crowd of spectators gave additional spirit to the combatants, so the cloud of witnesses who have themselves been in the same contest, ought to increase our earnestness, testifying, as they do, to God's faithfulness.<div eID="gen39155" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen39156" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">weight--</hi>As corporeal unwieldiness was, through a disciplinary diet, laid aside by candidates for the prize in racing; so carnal and worldly lusts, and all, whether from without or within, that would impede the heavenly runner, are the spiritual weight to be laid aside. "Encumbrance," all superfluous weight; the lust of the flesh, the lust of the eye, and the pride of life, and even harmless and otherwise useful things which would positively retard us (<reference osisRef="Mark.10.50">Mr 10:50</reference>, the blind man casting away his garment to come to Jesus; <reference osisRef="Mark.9.42-Mark.9.48">Mr 9:42-48</reference>; compare <reference osisRef="Eph.4.22">Ep 4:22</reference>; <reference osisRef="Col.3.9">Col 3:9</reference>, <reference osisRef="Col.3.10">10</reference>).<div eID="gen39156" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen39157" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">the sin which doth so easily beset us--</hi>Greek, "sin which easily stands around us"; so Luther, "which always so clings to us": "sinful propensity always surrounding us, ever present and ready" [Wahl]. It is not primarily "the sin," &c., but sin in general, with, however, special reference to "apostasy," against which he had already warned them, as one to which they might gradually be seduced; the besetting sin of the Hebrews, UNBELIEF.<div eID="gen39157" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen39158" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">with patience--</hi>Greek, "in persevering endurance" (<reference osisRef="Heb.10.36">He 10:36</reference>). On "run" compare <reference osisRef="1Cor.9.24">1Co 9:24</reference>, <reference osisRef="1Cor.9.25">25</reference>. <div eID="gen39158" type="x-p"/>
entries.0b3a67f18997e3f50094741f53c158ee363c129c: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv18567"/><div sID="gen39159" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv18567"/><hi type="bold">2. Looking unto--</hi>literally, "Looking from afar" (see on <reference osisRef="Heb.11.26">He 11:26</reference>); fixing the eyes upon Jesus seated on the throne of God.<div eID="gen39159" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen39160" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">author--</hi>"Prince-leader." The same Greek is translated, "Captain (of salvation)," <reference osisRef="Heb.2.10">He 2:10</reference>; "Prince (of life)," <reference osisRef="Acts.3.15">Ac 3:15</reference>. Going before us as the Originator of our faith, and the Leader whose matchless example we are to follow always. In this He is distinguished from all those examples of faith in <reference osisRef="Heb.11.2-Heb.11.40">He 11:2-40</reference>. (Compare <reference osisRef="1Cor.11.1">1Co 11:1</reference>). On His "faith" compare <reference osisRef="Heb.2.13">He 2:13</reference>; <reference osisRef="2Cor.3.12">3:12</reference>. Believers have ever looked to Him (<reference osisRef="Heb.11.26">He 11:26</reference>; <reference osisRef="Heb.13.8">13:8</reference>).<div eID="gen39160" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen39161" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">finisher--</hi>Greek, "Perfecter," referring to <reference osisRef="Heb.11.40">He 11:40</reference>.<div eID="gen39161" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen39162" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">of our faith--</hi>rather as Greek, "of the faith," including both His faith (as exhibited in what follows) and our faith. He fulfilled the ideal of faith Himself, and so, both as a vicarious offering and an example, He is the object of our faith.<div eID="gen39162" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen39163" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">for the joy ... set before him--</hi>namely, of presently after sitting down at the right hand of the throne of God; including besides His own personal joy, the joy of sitting there as a Prince and Saviour, to give repentance and remission of sins. The coming joy disarmed of its sting the present pain.<div eID="gen39163" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen39164" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">cross ... shame--</hi>the great stumbling-block to the Hebrews. "Despised," that is, disregarded. <div eID="gen39164" type="x-p"/>
entries.c6778fb5776dcb175c0e5971a8bf45d58cbe7ef7: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv18568"/><div sID="gen39165" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv18568"/><hi type="bold">3. For--</hi>justifying his exhortation, "Looking unto Jesus."<div eID="gen39165" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen39166" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">consider--</hi>by way of comparison with yourselves, so the Greek.<div eID="gen39166" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen39167" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">contradiction--</hi>unbelief, and every kind of opposition (<reference osisRef="Acts.28.19">Ac 28:19</reference>).<div eID="gen39167" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen39168" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">sinners--</hi>Sin assails us. Not sin, but sinners, contradicted Christ [Bengel].<div eID="gen39168" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen39169" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">be wearied and faint--</hi>Greek, "lest ye weary fainting." Compare <reference osisRef="Isa.49.4">Is 49:4</reference>, <reference osisRef="Isa.49.5">5</reference>, as a specimen of Jesus not being wearied out by the contradiction and strange unbelief of those among whom He labored, preaching as never man did, and exhibiting miracles wrought by His inherent power, as none else could do. <div eID="gen39169" type="x-p"/>
entries.1b9bd898c2da493d4f09a50ff400527b3224531a: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv18569"/><div sID="gen39170" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv18569"/><hi type="bold">4. not yet resisted unto blood--</hi>image from pugilism, as he previously had the image of a race, both being taken from the great national Greek games. Ye have suffered the loss of goods, and been a gazing-stock by reproaches and afflictions; ye have not shed your blood (see on <reference osisRef="Heb.13.7">He 13:7</reference>). "The athlete who hath seen his own blood, and who, though cast down by his opponent, does not let his spirits be cast down, who as often as he hath fallen hath risen the more determined, goes down to the encounter with great hope" [Seneca].<div eID="gen39170" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen39171" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">against sin--</hi>Sin is personified as an adversary; sin, whether within you, leading you to spare your blood, or in our adversaries, leading them to shed it, if they cannot through your faithfulness even unto blood, induce you to apostatize. <div eID="gen39171" type="x-p"/>
entries.ca6dde345337ed2f92a2ed11a95d07d1bcfe94ff: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv18570"/><div sID="gen39172" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv18570"/><hi type="bold">5. forgotten--</hi>"utterly," so the Greek. Compare <reference osisRef="Heb.12.15-Heb.12.17">He 12:15-17</reference>, in which he implies how utterly some of them had forgotten God's word. His exhortation ought to have more effect on you than the cheers and exhortations of the spectators have on the competitors striving in the games.<div eID="gen39172" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen39173" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">which--</hi>Greek, "the which," of which the following is a specimen [Alford].<div eID="gen39173" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen39174" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">speaketh unto you--</hi>as in a dialogue or discourse, so the Greek, implying God's loving condescension (compare <reference osisRef="Isa.1.18">Is 1:18</reference>).<div eID="gen39174" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen39175" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">despise not--</hi>literally, "Do not hold of little account." Betraying a contumacious spirit of unbelief (<reference osisRef="Heb.3.12">He 3:12</reference>), as "faint" implies a broken-down, weak, and desponding spirit. "Chastening" is to be borne with "subjection" (<reference osisRef="Heb.12.9">He 12:9</reference>); "rebuke" (more severe than chastening) is to be borne with endurance (<reference osisRef="Heb.12.7">He 12:7</reference>). "Some in adversity kick against God's will, others despond; neither is to be done by the Christian, who is peculiarly the child of God. To him such adverse things occur only by the decree of God, and that designed in kindness, namely, to remove the defilements adhering to the believer, and to exercise his patience" [Grotius]. <div eID="gen39175" type="x-p"/>
entries.c1c73679ee18eb9640c743ad11a16e327d9e2673: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv18571"/><div sID="gen39176" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv18571"/>6. (<reference osisRef="Rev.3.19">Re 3:19</reference>.)<div eID="gen39176" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen39177" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">and--</hi>Greek, "yea and," "and moreover"; bringing out an additional circumstance.<div eID="gen39177" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen39178" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">scourgeth--</hi>which draws forth "blood" (<reference osisRef="Heb.12.4">He 12:4</reference>).<div eID="gen39178" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen39179" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">receiveth--</hi>accepts. Takes to Himself as a son "in whom He delighteth" (<reference osisRef="Prov.3.12">Pr 3:12</reference>). <div eID="gen39179" type="x-p"/>
entries.db16f7f0d878da8295c1e99235e4eb9f318710ab: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv18572"/><div sID="gen39180" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv18572"/>7. In <reference osisRef="Heb.12.7">He 12:7</reference>, <reference osisRef="Heb.12.8">8</reference> the need of "chastening" or "discipline" is inculcated; in <reference osisRef="Heb.12.9">He 12:9</reference>, the duty of those to whom it is administered.<div eID="gen39180" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen39181" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">If--</hi>The oldest manuscripts read, "With a view to chastening (that is, since God's chastisement is with a view to your chastening, that is, disciplinary amelioration) endure patiently"; so Vulgate. Alford translates it as indicative, not so well, "It is for chastisement that ye are enduring."<div eID="gen39181" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen39182" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">dealeth with you--</hi>"beareth Himself toward you" in the very act of chastening.<div eID="gen39182" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen39183" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">what son is he--</hi>"What son is there" even in ordinary life? Much more God as to His sons (<reference osisRef="Isa.48.10">Is 48:10</reference>; <reference osisRef="Acts.14.22">Ac 14:22</reference>). The most eminent of God's saints were the most afflicted. God leads them by a way they know not (<reference osisRef="Isa.42.16">Is 42:16</reference>). We too much look at each trial by itself, instead of taking it in connection with the whole plan of our salvation, as if a traveller were to complain of the steepness and roughness of one turn in the path, without considering that it led him into green pastures, on the direct road to the city of habitation. The New Testament alone uses the Greek term for education (paideia), to express "discipline" or correction, as of a child by a wise father. <div eID="gen39183" type="x-p"/>
entries.186c721fe42b860509def760ee01bff4c462da42: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv18573"/><div sID="gen39184" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv18573"/><hi type="bold">8. if ye be without--</hi>excluded from participation in chastisement, and wishing to be so.<div eID="gen39184" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen39185" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">all--</hi>all sons: all the worthies enumerated in the eleventh chapter: all the witnesses (<reference osisRef="Heb.12.1">He 12:1</reference>).<div eID="gen39185" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen39186" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">are--</hi>Greek, "have been made."<div eID="gen39186" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen39187" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">then are ye bastards--</hi>of whom their fathers take no care whether they are educated or not; whereas every right-minded father is concerned for the moral well-being of his legitimate son. "Since then not to be chastised is a mark of bastardy, we ought [not to refuse, but] rejoice in chastisement, as a mark of our genuine sonship" [Chrysostom]. <div eID="gen39187" type="x-p"/>
entries.eb7ca729e62563634a5ffccd57e7c0e0421f9cb1: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv18574"/><div sID="gen39188" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv18574"/><hi type="bold">9. fathers ... which corrected us--</hi>rather as Greek, "We had the fathers of our flesh as correctors."<div eID="gen39188" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen39189" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">subjection--</hi>See the punishment of insubordination, <reference osisRef="Deut.21.18">De 21:18</reference>.<div eID="gen39189" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen39190" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">Father of spirits--</hi>contrasted with "the fathers of our flesh." "Generation by men is carnal, by God is spiritual" [Bengel]. As "Father of spirits," He is both the Originator, and the Providential and Gracious Sustainer, at once of animal and spiritual life. Compare "and LIVE," namely, spiritually; also <reference osisRef="Heb.12.10">He 12:10</reference>, "that we might be partakers of His holiness" (<reference osisRef="2Pet.1.4">2Pe 1:4</reference>). God is a spirit Himself, and the Creator of spirits like Himself, in contrast to men who are flesh, and the progenitors of flesh (<reference osisRef="John.3.6">Joh 3:6</reference>). Jesus our pattern "learned obedience" experimentally by suffering (<reference osisRef="Heb.5.8">He 5:8</reference>).<div eID="gen39190" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen39191" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">and live--</hi>and so, thereby live spiritually and eternally. <div eID="gen39191" type="x-p"/>
entries.0634483388a5190d454f34bcdc74d440b37c59b2: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv18575"/><div sID="gen39192" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv18575"/>10. Showing wherein the chastisement of our heavenly Father is preferable to that of earthly fathers.<div eID="gen39192" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen39193" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">for a few days--</hi>that is, with a view to our well-being in the few days of our earthly life: so the Greek.<div eID="gen39193" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen39194" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">after their own pleasure--</hi>Greek, "according to what seemed fit to themselves." Their rule of chastening is what may seem fit to their own often erring judgment, temper, or caprice. The two defects of human education are: (1) the prevalence in it of a view to the interests of our short earthly term of days; (2) the absence in parents of the unerring wisdom of our heavenly Father. "They err much at one time in severity, at another in indulgence [1Sa 3:13; Ep 6:4], and do not so much chasten as THINK they chasten" [Bengel].<div eID="gen39194" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen39195" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">that we might be partakers of his holiness--</hi>becoming holy as He is holy (<reference osisRef="John.15.2">Joh 15:2</reference>). To become holy like God is tantamount to being educated for passing eternity with God (<reference osisRef="Heb.12.14">He 12:14</reference>; <reference osisRef="2Pet.1.4">2Pe 1:4</reference>). So this "partaking of God's holiness" stands in contrast to the "few days" of this life, with a view to which earthly fathers generally educate their sons. <div eID="gen39195" type="x-p"/>
entries.0e793d11f211ee829791269fa2424f1d80f97c21: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv18576"/><div sID="gen39196" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv18576"/><hi type="bold">11. joyous ... grievous--</hi>Greek, "matter of joy ... matter of grief." The objection that chastening is grievous is here anticipated and answered. It only seems so to those being chastened, whose judgments are confused by the present pain. Its ultimate fruit amply compensates for any temporary pam. The real object of the fathers in chastening is not that they find pleasure in the children's pain. Gratified wishes, our Father knows, would often be our real curses.<div eID="gen39196" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen39197" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">fruit of righteousness--</hi>righteousness (in practice, springing from faith) is the fruit which chastening, the tree yields (<reference osisRef="Phil.1.11">Php 1:11</reference>). "Peaceable" (compare <reference osisRef="Isa.32.17">Is 32:17</reference>): in contrast to the ordeal of conflict by which it has been won. "Fruit of righteousness to be enjoyed in peace after the conflict" [Tholuck]. As the olive garland, the emblem of peace as well as victory, was put on the victor's brow in the games.<div eID="gen39197" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen39198" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">exercised thereby--</hi>as athletes exercised in training for a contest. Chastisement is the exercise to give experience, and make the spiritual combatant irresistibly victorious (<reference osisRef="Rom.5.3">Ro 5:3</reference>). "Oh, happy the servant for whose improvement his Lord is earnest, with whom he deigns to be angry, whom He does not deceive by dissembling admonition" (withholding admonition, and so leading the man to think he needs it not)! [Tertullian, Patience, 11]. Observe the "afterwards"; that is the time often when God works. <div eID="gen39198" type="x-p"/>
entries.d62dcb4749b69f2429249ef91882aba21df3d022: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv18577"/><div sID="gen39199" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv18577"/>12. He addresses them as runners in a race, and pugilists, and warriors [Chrysostom]. The "wherefore" is resumed from <reference osisRef="Heb.12.1">He 12:1</reference>.<div eID="gen39199" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen39200" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">lift up--</hi>In <reference osisRef="Isa.35.3">Is 35:3</reference>, from which Paul here quotes, it is, "Strengthen ye the weak hands." The hand is the symbol of one's strength. Alford translates, "Put straight again the relaxed hands." English Version expresses the sense well.<div eID="gen39200" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen39201" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">feeble--</hi>literally, "paralyzed"; a word used only by Luke, Paul's companion, in the New Testament. The exhortation has three parts: the first relates to ourselves, <reference osisRef="Heb.12.12">He 12:12</reference>, <reference osisRef="Heb.12.13">13</reference>; the second, to others, <reference osisRef="Heb.12.14">He 12:14</reference>, "peace with all men"; the third, to God, "holiness, without which," &c. The first is referred to in <reference osisRef="Heb.12.15">He 12:15</reference>, "test any man fail of the grace of God"; the second in the words, "lest any root of bitterness," &c.; the third in <reference osisRef="Heb.12.16">He 12:16</reference>, "Lest there be any fornicator or profane person," &c. This threefold relation often occurs in Paul's Epistles. Compare Note, see on <reference osisRef="Titus.2.12">Tit 2:12</reference>, "soberly, righteously, and godly." The Greek active verb, not the middle or reflexive, requires the sense to be, Lift up not only your own hands and knees, but also those of your brethren (compare <reference osisRef="Heb.12.15">He 12:15</reference>; <reference osisRef="Isa.35.4">Is 35:4</reference>). <div eID="gen39201" type="x-p"/>
entries.a9cd08b31e7c257859620b9e8f356d247611bf7a: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv18578"/><div sID="gen39202" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv18578"/>13. Quoted from <reference osisRef="Prov.4.26">Pr 4:26</reference>, Septuagint, "Make straight paths for thy feet."<div eID="gen39202" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen39203" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">straight--</hi>that is, leading by a straight road to joy and grace (<reference osisRef="Heb.12.1">He 12:1</reference>, 2, 15). Cease to "halt" between Judaism and Christianity [Bengel].<div eID="gen39203" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen39204" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">paths--</hi>literally, "wheel tracks." Let your walk be so firm and so unanimous in the right direction that a plain track and "highway" may be thereby established for those who accompany and follow you, to perceive and walk in (<reference osisRef="Isa.35.8">Is 35:8</reference>) [Alford].<div eID="gen39204" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen39205" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">that which is lame--</hi>those "weak in the faith" (<reference osisRef="Rom.14.1">Ro 14:1</reference>), having still Judaizing prejudices.<div eID="gen39205" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen39206" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">be turned out of the way--</hi>(<reference osisRef="Prov.4.27">Pr 4:27</reference>); and, so missing the way, lose the prize of "the race" (<reference osisRef="Heb.12.1">He 12:1</reference>).<div eID="gen39206" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen39207" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">rather he healed--</hi>Proper exercise of itself contributes to health; the habit of walking straight onward in the right way tends to healing. <div eID="gen39207" type="x-p"/>
entries.074d13f551d5ef38adf3aed6d7539db0b7358462: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv18579"/><div sID="gen39208" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv18579"/><hi type="bold">14. follow peace with all men--</hi>with the brethren especially (<reference osisRef="Rom.14.19">Ro 14:19</reference>), that so the "lame" among them be not "turned out of the way" (<reference osisRef="Heb.12.13">He 12:13</reference>), and that no one of them "fail of the grace of God" (<reference osisRef="Heb.12.15">He 12:15</reference>).<div eID="gen39208" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen39209" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">holiness--</hi>a distinct Greek word from God's "holiness" (<reference osisRef="Heb.12.10">He 12:10</reference>). Translate here "sanctification." His is absolute holiness: our part is to put on His holiness, becoming "holy as He is holy," by sanctification. While "following peace with all men," we are not so to seek to please them, as to make God's will and our sanctification a secondary object; this latter must be our first aim. (<reference osisRef="Gal.1.10">Ga 1:10</reference>).<div eID="gen39209" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen39210" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">without which--</hi>Greek, "apart from which."<div eID="gen39210" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen39211" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">no man shall see the Lord--</hi>no man as a son; in heavenly glory (<reference osisRef="Rev.22.3">Re 22:3</reference>, <reference osisRef="Rev.22.4">4</reference>). In the East, none but the greatest favorites are admitted to the honor of seeing the king (compare <reference osisRef="2Sam.14.24">2Sa 14:24</reference>). The Lord being pure and holy, none but the pure and holy shall see Him (<reference osisRef="Matt.5.8">Mt 5:8</reference>). Without holiness in them, they could not enjoy Him who is holiness itself (<reference osisRef="Zech.14.20">Zec 14:20</reference>). The connection of purity with seeing the Lord, appears in <reference osisRef="1John.3.2">1Jo 3:2</reference>, <reference osisRef="1John.3.3">3</reference>; <reference osisRef="Eph.5.5">Ep 5:5</reference>. Contrast <reference osisRef="Heb.12.16">He 12:16</reference> (compare <reference osisRef="1Thess.4.3">1Th 4:3</reference>). In <reference osisRef="Matt.24.30">Mt 24:30</reference>; <reference osisRef="Rev.1.7">Re 1:7</reference>, it is said that all shall see the Lord; but, that shall be as a Judge, not as their lasting portion and God, which is meant here. The Greek verb does not denote the mere action of seeing, but the seer's state of mind to which the object is presented: so in <reference osisRef="Matt.5.8">Mt 5:8</reference> they shall truly comprehend God [Tittmann]. None but the holy could appreciate the holy God, none else therefore shall abide in His presence. "The bad shall only see Him in His form as Son of man [compare <reference osisRef="Rev.1.13">Re 1:13</reference>, with <reference osisRef="Rev.1.7">Re 1:7</reference>; and <reference osisRef="Matt.24.30">Mt 24:30</reference>; <reference osisRef="Acts.1.11">Ac 1:11</reference>; 17:31]; still it will be in the glory in which He shall judge, not in the lowliness in which He was judged. His form as God, wherein He is equal to the Father, without doubt the ungodly shall not see; for it is only 'the pure in heart who shall see God'" [Augustine]. "He shall come to judge, who stood before a judge. He shall come in the form in which He was judged, that they may see Him whom they pierced: He who was before hidden shall come manifested in power: He, as Judge, shall condemn the real culprits, who was Himself falsely made a culprit." <div eID="gen39211" type="x-p"/>
entries.75256ee70187b282b6877c021e51b544e34fce6e: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv18580"/><div sID="gen39212" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv18580"/><hi type="bold">15. lest any ... fall--</hi>Greek, "lest any (namely, through sloth in running) failing," or "falling short of the grace of God ... trouble you." The image is taken from a company of travellers, one of whom lags behind, and so never reaches the end of the long and laborious journey [Chrysostom].<div eID="gen39212" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen39213" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">root of bitterness--</hi>not merely a "bitter root," which might possibly bring forth sweet fruits; this, a root whose essence is "bitterness," never could. Paul here refers to <reference osisRef="Deut.29.18">De 29:18</reference>, "Lest there should be among you a root that beareth gall and wormwood" (compare <reference osisRef="Acts.8.23">Ac 8:23</reference>). Root of bitterness comprehends every person (compare <reference osisRef="Heb.12.16">He 12:16</reference>) and every principle of doctrine or practice so radically corrupt as to spread corruption all around. The only safety is in rooting out such a root of bitterness.<div eID="gen39213" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen39214" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">many--</hi>rather, "the many," that is, the whole congregation. So long as it is hidden under the earth it cannot be remedied, but when it "springs up," it must be dealt with boldly. Still remember the caution (<reference osisRef="Matt.13.26-Matt.13.30">Mt 13:26-30</reference>) as to rooting out persons. No such danger can arise in rooting out bad principles. <div eID="gen39214" type="x-p"/>
entries.aa9dc4ca238af5ec48ec619b333c7029ae3dd77a: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv18581"/><div sID="gen39215" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv18581"/><hi type="bold">16. fornicator--</hi>(<reference osisRef="Heb.13.4">He 13:4</reference>; <reference osisRef="1Cor.10.8">1Co 10:8</reference>).<div eID="gen39215" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen39216" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">or profane--</hi>Fornication is nearly akin to gluttony, Esau's sin. He profanely cast away his spiritual privilege for the gratification of his palate. <reference osisRef="Gen.25.34">Ge 25:34</reference> graphically portrays him. An example well fitted to strike needful horror into the Hebrews, whosoever of them, like Esau, were only sons of Isaac according to the flesh [Bengel].<div eID="gen39216" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen39217" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">for one morsel--</hi>The smallness of the inducement only aggravates the guilt of casting away eternity for such a trifle, so far is it from being a claim for mercy (compare <reference osisRef="Gen.3.6">Ge 3:6</reference>). One single act has often the greatest power either for good or for evil. So in the cases of Reuben and Saul, for evil (<reference osisRef="Gen.49.4">Ge 49:4</reference>; <reference osisRef="1Chr.5.1">1Ch 5:1</reference>; <reference osisRef="1Sam.13.12-1Sam.13.14">1Sa 13:12-14</reference>); and, on the other hand, for good, Abraham and Phinehas (<reference osisRef="Gen.12.1">Ge 12:1</reference>, &c.; <reference osisRef="Gen.15.5">Ge 15:5</reference>, <reference osisRef="Gen.15.6">6</reference>; <reference osisRef="Num.25.6-Num.25.15">Nu 25:6-15</reference>).<div eID="gen39217" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen39218" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">his birthright--</hi>Greek, "his own (so the oldest manuscripts read, intensifying the suicidal folly and sin of the act) rights of primogeniture," involving the high spiritual privilege of being ancestor of the promised seed, and heir of the promises in Him. The Hebrews whom Paul addressed, had, as Christians, the spiritual rights of primogeniture (compare <reference osisRef="Heb.12.23">He 12:23</reference>): he intimates that they must exercise holy self-control, if they wish not, like Esau, to forfeit them. <div eID="gen39218" type="x-p"/>
