We hence see the propriety of “the whole assembly,” or the whole number of the faithful, composed of Jews or Gentiles. The Apostle says, “We are part of this whole assembly,” and in order to point out his meaning more distinctly he calls it “the Church.” The reference here seems to be the saints on earth, and at the end of the verse to departed saints. And they are said to be “made perfect,” because freed from guilt, sin, and every pollution, having “washed their robes in the blood of the Lamb.” — <hi type="italic">Ed</hi>.<div eID="gen133988" type="x-p"/> </note><div eID="gen133987" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen133989" type="x-p"/><hi type="italic">The judge of all,</hi> <hi type="italic">etc.</hi> This seems to have been said to inspire fear, as though he had said, that grace is in such a way altered to us, that we ought still to consider that we have to do with a judge, to whom an account must be given if we presumptuously intrude into his sanctuary polluted and profane.<div eID="gen133989" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen133990" type="x-p"/><hi type="italic">The spirits of just men,</hi> <hi type="italic">etc.</hi> He adds this to intimate that we are joined to holy souls, which have put off their bodies, and left behind them all the filth of this world; and hence he says that they are consecrated or “made perfect”, for they are no more subject to the infirmities of the flesh, having laid aside the flesh itself. And hence we may with certainty conclude, that pious souls, separated from their bodies, still live with God, for we could not possibly be otherwise joined to them as companions.<div eID="gen133990" type="x-p"/> <div annotateRef="Bible:Heb.12.23" annotateType="commentary" eID="gen133986" osisID="Heb.12.23" type="section"/>
entries.cceea467b0a2a55a5f3e9b62ee87087280f5babf:
24. And to Jesus the Mediator, etc. He adds this in the last place, because it is he alone through whom the Father is reconciled to us, and who renders his face serene and lovely to us, so that we may come to him without fear. At the same time he shows how Christ becomes our Mediator, even through his own blood, which after the Hebrew mode of speaking he calls the blood of sprinkling, which means sprinkled blood; for as it was once for all shed to make an atonement for us, so our souls must be now cleansed by it through faith. At the same time the Apostle alludes to the ancient rite of the Law, which has been before mentioned.
That speaketh better things, etc. There is no reason why better may not be rendered adverbially in the following manner, — “Christ’s blood cries more efficaciously, and is better heard by God than the blood of Abel.” It is, however, preferable to take the words literally: the blood of Christ is said to speak better things, because it avails to obtain pardon for our sins. The blood of Abel did not properly cry out; for it was his murder that called for vengeance before God. But the blood of Christ cries out, and the atonement made by it is heard daily.
See Appendix X 2.
Hebrews Chapter 12:25-29
25. See that ye refuse not him that speaketh. For if they escaped not who refused him that spake on earth, much more shall not we escape, if we turn away from him that speaketh from heaven:
25. Videte ne asperenemini loquentem; nam si illi, qui aspeernati sunt eum qui loquebatur in terra, non effugerunt, multo magic nos si aversemur loquentem e coelis;
26. Whose voice then shook the earth: but now he hath promised, saying, Yet once more I shake not the earth only, but also heaven.
26. Cujus vox tune terram concussit, nunc autem denuntiavit, dicens, Adhuc semel ego moveo non solum terram, sed etiam coelum.
27. And this word, Yet once more, signifieth the removing of those things that are shaken, as of things that are made, that those things which cannot be shaken may remain.
27. Illud autem, Adhuc semel, significat eurum quae concutiuntur translationem, ut maneant quae non concutiuntur.
28. Wherefore we receiving a kingdom which cannot be moved, let us have grace, whereby we may serve God acceptably with reverence and godly fear:
28. Quare regnum quod non concutitur apprehendentes, habemus (alias, habeumus) gratiam: per quam colamus Deum, placentes illi cum reverentia et religione:
29. For our God is a consuming fire.
29. Deus enim noster ignis consumens est.
entries.0ff461b6bbf58791abec1181d1c9c4f3b0eebb2f: <div annotateRef="Bible:Heb.12.25" annotateType="commentary" osisID="Heb.12.25" sID="gen134008" type="section"/> <div sID="gen134009" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">25.</hi> <hi type="italic">See that ye refuse not him that speaketh,</hi> <hi type="italic">etc.</hi> He uses the same verb as before, when he said that the people entreated that God should not speak to them; but he means as I think, another thing, even that we ought not to reject the word destined for us. He further shows what he had in view in the last comparison, even that the severest punishment awaits the despisers of the Gospel, since the ancients under the Law did not despise it with impunity. And he pursues the argument from the less to the greater, when he says, that God or Moses spoke then on earth, but that the same God or Christ speaks now from heaven. At the same time I prefer regarding God in both instances as the speaker. And he is said to have spoken on earth, because he spoke in a lower strain. Let us ever bear in mind that he refers to the external ministration of the Law, which, as compared with the gospel, partook of what was earthly, and did not lead men’s minds above the heavens unto perfect wisdom; for though the Law contained in it the same truth, yet as it was only a training school, perfection could not belong to it. <note n="269"> <div sID="gen134010" type="x-p"/> By “him that speaketh,” is by some understood Christ, but more properly God, as his is the leading subject in the foregoing and the following verses. The words which follow are brief; and the first clause is explained more fully in <reference osisRef="Bible:Heb.10.28">chapter 10:28</reference>, and the second in <reference osisRef="Bible:Heb.1.2">chapter 1:2</reference>. God spake “on earth” by Moses, but “from heaven” by his son, who came from heaven, ascended into heaven and sent his spirit down from heaven. The comparison here is between speaking on earth and speaking from heaven; but included in this, as previously explained in the Epistle, are the agents employed. God in delivering the Law fixed on a place on earth, and then as it were descended and employed an earthly agent, a mere man as his mediator; but in delivering the gospel, he did not descend from heaven, but employed a heavenly agent, his own son; thus manifested the superiority of the Gospel over the law. And that God is meant throughout this verse is evident from the following verse, “Whose voice,” etc. The passage may be thus rendered, —<div eID="gen134010" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen134011" type="x-p"/>“See that ye reject not him who speaketh; for if they escaped not who rejected him when speaking on earth, how much more shall not we, if we turn away from him when speaking from heaven?”<div eID="gen134011" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen134012" type="x-p"/>We have no single word to express χρηματίζοντα — oraculizing, rendered by Doddridge, “giving forth oracles;” by Macknight, “delivering an oracle;” and by Stuart, “warning.” But the best word we can adopt here is “speaking.” — <hi type="italic">Ed</hi><div eID="gen134012" type="x-p"/> </note><div eID="gen134009" type="x-p"/> <div annotateRef="Bible:Heb.12.25" annotateType="commentary" eID="gen134008" osisID="Heb.12.25" type="section"/>
entries.54f3e1ef5de166a1ae0367ac1dd041d1f35be364: <div annotateRef="Bible:Heb.12.26" annotateType="commentary" osisID="Heb.12.26" sID="gen134013" type="section"/> <div sID="gen134014" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">26.</hi> <hi type="italic">Whose voice then shook the earth,</hi> <hi type="italic">etc.</hi> Though God shook the earth when he published his Law, yet he shows that he now speaks more gloriously, for he shakes both earth and heaven. He quotes on the subject the testimony of the Prophet Haggai, though he gives not the words literally; but as the Prophet foretells a future shaking of the earth and the heaven, the Apostle borrows the idea in order to teach us that the voice of the Gospel not only thunders through the earth, but also penetrates above the heavens. But that the Prophet speaks of Christ’s kingdom, is beyond any dispute, for it immediately follows in the same passage, “I will shake all nations; and come shall the desire of all nations, and I will fill this house with glory.” It is however certain that neither all nations have been gathered into one body, except under the banner of Christ, nor has there been any desire in which we ought to acquiesce but Christ alone, nor was the temple of Solomon exceeded in glory until the magnificence of Christ became known through the whole world. The Prophet then no doubt refers to the time of Christ. But if at the commencement of Christ’s kingdom, not only the lower parts of the world were shaken, but his power also reached the heaven, the Apostle justly concludes that the doctrine of the Gospel is sublimer than that of the Law, and ought to be more distinctly heard by all creatures. <note n="270"> <div sID="gen134015" type="x-p"/> The quotation is literally neither from Hebrew nor from the Sept., but is substantially the same. “The earth and the heaven” may be deemed a phrase used to designate the whole state of things, as they include the whole of the visible creation. The whole Jewish polity, civil and religious, is generally supposed to be intended here. But as the shaking of the nations is mentioned in <reference osisRef="Bible:Hag.2.6 Bible:Hag.2.7">Haggai 2:6, 7</reference>, Macknight thought that by “the earth” is meant heathen idolatry, and by “heaven” the Jewish economy, so called because it was divinely appointed. If this be allowed, then we see a reason for the change which the Apostle has made in the words: the original is both in Hebrew and in the Sept., “I shake (or will shake) the heaven and the earth;” but the Apostle says: “I shake not only the earth, but the heaven also.” — <hi type="italic">Ed</hi>.<div eID="gen134015" type="x-p"/> </note><div eID="gen134014" type="x-p"/> <div annotateRef="Bible:Heb.12.26" annotateType="commentary" eID="gen134013" osisID="Heb.12.26" type="section"/>
entries.d7cc8099adf550005cc9f640607bf7db0564ddd6:
27. And this word, yet once more, etc. The words of the Prophet are these, “Yet a little while;” and he means that the calamity of the people would not be perpetual, but that the Lord would succor them. But the Apostle lays no stress on this expression; he only infers from the shaking of the heaven and the earth that the state of the world was to be changed at the coming of Christ; for things created are subject to decay, but Christ’s kingdom is eternal; then all creatures must needs be brought into a better state.
See Appendix Y 2.
He makes hence a transition to another exhortation, that we are to lay hold on that kingdom which cannot be shaken; for the Lord shakes us for this end, that he may really and forever establish us in himself. At the same time I prefer a different reading, which is given by the ancient Latin version, “Receiving a kingdom, we have grace,” etc. When read affirmatively, the passage runs best, — “We, in embracing the Gospel, have the gift of the Spirit of Christ, that we may reverently and devoutly worship God.” If it be read as an exhortation, “Let us have,” it is a strained and obscure mode of speaking. The Apostle means in short, as I think, that provided we enter by faith into Christ’s kingdom, we shall enjoy constant grace, which will effectually retain us in the service of God; for as the kingdom of Christ is above the world, so is the gift of regeneration.
See Appendix Z 2.
By saying that God is to be served acceptably, εὐαρέστως, with reverence and fear, he intimates that though he requires us to serve with promptitude and delight, there is yet no service approved by him except it be united with humility and due reverence. Thus he condemns froward confidence of the flesh, as well as the sloth which also proceeds from it.
The Vulgate is, “with fear and reverence;” Beza’s “with modesty and reverence and religious fear;” Schleusner’s, “with reverence and devotion.” Stuart has adopted our version. See Appendix A 3. — Ed.
entries.79d7f4ff37ff139198eb9d4fcc17398e957b2ba3:
29. For our God, etc. As he had before kindly set before us the grace of God, so he now makes known his severity; and he seems to have borrowed this sentence from the fourth chapter of Deuteronomy. Thus we see that God omits nothing by which he may draw us to himself; he begins indeed with love and kindness, so that we may follow him the more willingly; but when by alluring he effects but little, he terrifies us.
And doubtless it is expedient that the grace of God should never be promised to us without being accompanied with threatening; for we are so extremely prone to indulge ourselves, that without the application of these stimulants the milder doctrine would prove ineffectual. Then the Lord, as he is propitious and merciful to such as fear him unto a thousand generations; so he is a jealous God and a just avenger, when despised, unto the third and the fourth generation.
The conjunction καὶ at the beginning of this verse is commonly omitted by translators, but Macknight has retained it, “For even our God,” etc. The intimation clearly is, that under the Gospel no less than under the Law God is a consuming fire to apostates; and apostasy or idolatry is the sin especially referred to in Deuteronomy 4:24, from which this passage is taken. — Ed
CHAPTER 13
Hebrews Chapter 13:1-6
1. Let brotherly love continue.
1. Fraterna charitas maneat.
2. Be not forgetful to entertain strangers: for thereby some have entertained angels unawares.
2. Hospitalitatis ne sitis immemores; per hanc enim quosdam latuit quum recipissent Angelos.
3. Remember them that are in bonds, as bound with them; and them which suffer adversity, as being yourselves also in the body.
3. Memores estote vinctorum, tanquam ipsi quoque sitis in corpore.
4. Marriage is honourable in all, and the bed undefiled: but whoremongers and adulterers God will judge.
4. Honorabile in omnibus conjugium et thorus impollutus; scortatores auten et adulteros judicabit Deus.
5. Let your conversation be without covetousness; and be content with such things as ye have: for he hath said, I will never leave thee, nor forsake thee.
5. Sint mores sine avaritia: contenti sitis iis quae adsunt; ipse enim dixit, Non te desero, neque te derelinquo:
6. So that we may boldly say, The Lord is my helper, and I will not fear what man shall do unto me.
6. Ut fidentes dicamus, Dominus mihi adjutor, neque timebo quid faciat mihi homo.

               <ns0:p n="17">17 For <ns0:note n="w" place="bottom">As <ns0:hi>Esau</ns0:hi>'s Sin was, such was his Penalty; <ns0:hi>for they knew,</ns0:hi> and were well acquainted with this in <ns0:hi>Moses</ns0:hi>'s History of him, That after he had despised his Birth-right, and sold it, being at Man's Estate, <ns0:hi>Gen.</ns0:hi> 27. and was <ns0:hi>desirous to inherit</ns0:hi> that Bles<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />sing, he was <ns0:hi>rejected</ns0:hi> by his Father, as well as by God, and could not obtain it, being unalterably setled on <ns0:hi>Iacob</ns0:hi> by both.</ns0:note> ye know how that afterward when he would have inherited the blessing, he was re<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />jected: for he <ns0:note n="x" place="bottom">He <ns0:hi>found no place of Repentance,</ns0:hi> as to the giving it, <ns0:hi>with God</ns0:hi> who gave it, and would not alter it, <ns0:hi>Rom.</ns0:hi> 11.29. nor with <ns0:hi>his Father,</ns0:hi> who did not repent of giving it to <ns0:hi>Iacob,</ns0:hi> but confirmed it, <ns0:hi>Gen.</ns0:hi> 27.33, 40. and 28.1, 3, 4.                <ns0:p n="18">18 For <ns0:note n="y" place="bottom">
                     <ns0:hi>For,</ns0:hi> sheweth from this Verse to the 25th, the Apostle inforcing on these <ns0:hi>Hebrews,</ns0:hi> and with them on all Christians the <ns0:hi>Pursuit of Holiness and Peace,</ns0:hi> by subjoining the great helps they have for it, beyond what the Old-Testament-Church had, they being freed from the Legal Dispensation, which was less helpful to it, and admitted to that of the Gospel, most promoting it. The first he layeth down from <ns0:hi>v.</ns0:hi> 18, to 22. and the other from <ns0:hi>v.</ns0:hi> 22, to 25. They are freed from the Covenant-Dispensation at Mount <ns0:hi>Sinai.</ns0:hi>
                  </ns0:note> ye are not come <ns0:note n="z" place="bottom">You have not been called, as to your Body, to journey it to <ns0:hi>Si<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />nai,</ns0:hi> or as to your Faith to close with that Covenant-Admi<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />nistration, to depend on, or have any Expectation from it, as delivered by <ns0:hi>Moses</ns0:hi> at <ns0:hi>Mount Sinai</ns0:hi> in <ns0:hi>Arabia,</ns0:hi> a <ns0:hi>Mountain</ns0:hi> visible, tactible, sensible, on earth; signifying the Covenant-Dispen<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />sation from this Mount to be low, and earthy, occasioning earthy Thoughts of God, and carriage to him, sticking in an earthy Altar-Sacrifice, and carnal, and sensual Religion, to the Law written in Stones, without minding the Spirituali<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ty of it, or having it in Hearts, walking wisely in this Wil<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />derness-state, yet by the Charge of God, not touchable by <ns0:hi>Israel</ns0:hi> at that time, tho they came near to it in the third Month after their coming out of <ns0:hi>Egypt,</ns0:hi> Exod. 19.1, 12, 13, 23.</ns0:note> unto <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">Exod. 19.12, 18, 19.</ns0:note> the mount that might be touched, and <ns0:note n="a" place="bottom">To the Fire, in the which the Lord descended on the Mount, <ns0:hi>Exod.</ns0:hi> 19.18. which burnt unto the midst of Heaven, <ns0:hi>Deut.</ns0:hi> 4.11. and 5.23, 24. and would consume them that broke that Law, which he spake to them out of it, <ns0:hi>Deut.</ns0:hi> 33.2.</ns0:note> that burned with fire, nor unto <ns0:note n="b" place="bottom">To the black, thick <ns0:hi>Smoke</ns0:hi> that ascended as the Smoke of a Furnace, <ns0:hi>Exod.</ns0:hi> 19.18. to <ns0:hi>Darkness,</ns0:hi> occasioned by the thick Clouds enveloping the Mount, <ns0:hi>Deut.</ns0:hi> 4.11. and 5.23. <ns0:hi>to Tempest,</ns0:hi> the Storm of Thundering, and Lightnings, and Earthquake, the terrible Attendants of this Solemnity, <ns0:hi>Exod.</ns0:hi> 19.16, 18. and 20.18. All these shadowing forth the fiery and terrible Storms of Wrath and Indignation, which should pursue the breakers of this Covenant, to the lowest Hell; giving them in this Delivery of the Law, a visible Type of what should be the issue of their breaking it, <ns0:hi>Exod.</ns0:hi> 19.22, 24. These Terrors of the Almighty did so fright them, that they run from God, and set not themselves to the se<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />rious pursuit of Holiness, <ns0:hi>Isa.</ns0:hi> 33.14.</ns0:note> blackness, and darkness, and tempest;</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="19">
                  <ns0:pb facs="tcp:64193:569" />19 And <ns0:note n="c" place="bottom">Which was most shrill and dreadful, it sounded long, and waxed louder and louder, giving a fearful Alarm unto <ns0:hi>Israel</ns0:hi> to draw near to the Lord to hear his Law to them, and covenant with them, and to see a Type of their Doom, if they transgressed it, in an obscure Representation of the General Judgment, <ns0:hi>Exod.</ns0:hi> 19.16, 19. and 20.18. compare 1 <ns0:hi>Thess.</ns0:hi> 4.16. 2 <ns0:hi>Thess.</ns0:hi> 1.7, 8, 9.</ns0:note> the sound of a trumpet, and the voice of words, <ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#PDCC" extent="1 letter">
                     <ns0:desc>•</ns0:desc>
                  </ns0:gap>hich <ns0:hi>voice</ns0:hi> they that heard <ns0:note n="e" place="bottom">The People being overwhelmed with the Majesty and Dreadfulness of that Voice, deprecated any more such for matter or manner of Manifestation to them, <ns0:hi>Exod.</ns0:hi> 20.19. <ns0:hi>Deut.</ns0:hi> 5.23, 24, 25, 26. and <ns0:hi>ch.</ns0:hi> 18.16. And therefore desired <ns0:hi>Moses</ns0:hi> to speak to them God's Law, and that God might speak no more.</ns0:note>, <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">Exod. 20.19.</ns0:note> intreated that the word should not be spoken to them any more:<ns0:note n="d" place="bottom">After which Alarm, the Angel of the Covenant uttered his Voice out of the Fire most majestickly, distinctly, and loudly, spake to <ns0:hi>Israel</ns0:hi> in their own Language, the Ten Words, or Commandments, that they might hear and understand them, so as they sensed them to be dreadful for their sound and matter, <ns0:hi>Exod.</ns0:hi> 20.1, to 20. <ns0:hi>Deut.</ns0:hi> 4.10, 12, 13. and 5.1, to 28.</ns0:note>
               </ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="20">20 For <ns0:note n="f" place="bottom">The reason of the foregoing Deprecation, and which adds to the Terribleness of this Covenant-Dispensation; <ns0:hi>for</ns0:hi> the Voice surpassed their Strength and Capacity, that they must die, if they heard it any more; so dreadful was the sound and matter of it: for the Commandment and threat<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ning was, That if any Man or Beast did but as much as touch the Mountain, they should die for it, <ns0:hi>Exod.</ns0:hi> 19.12, 13, 21, 23, 24. Therefore was <ns0:hi>Moses</ns0:hi> so strictly charged to look to it, and to provide against it, shewing the Dreadfulness of that Covenant-Dispensation, that if Men did not keep their Beasts from coming near, they should be stoned, or darted to Death; how much more themselves, if they should transgress the Law, which, tho it was designed to lead them unto Christ, yet was not generally so discerned or used by them. So that if the Publication of it be so terrible, how much more the Punishment for breaking it? <ns0:hi>Exod.</ns0:hi> 20.20.</ns0:note> they could not endure that which was commanded. And if so much as a beast touch the mountain, it shall be stoned, or thrust through with a dart.</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="21">21 And <ns0:note n="g" place="bottom">It must needs be a dreadful, fearful, horrid, and asto<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />nishing Apparition, and Exhibition of the great Law-giver here, that such a Person as <ns0:hi>Moses,</ns0:hi> so sanctified by him, so favoured with Familiarity with him, so constituted Mediator between the People and God in this Work for their Good and Comfort, so called and ordered by God to manage it, yet should cry to God to succour him, while he did quake and tremble at it; and was comforted and strengthned by God's Voice to him again, <ns0:hi>Exod.</ns0:hi> 19.19. Christians now have no Call, nor Access to so terrible a Dispensation of the Covenant, but have Immunity, Exemption, and Freedom from it, which was not so helpful to Holiness, as the Go<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />spel-Dispensation, to which now they have actual Admission, having freed them from all the Terrors and Curses of the Mosaical one.</ns0:note> so terrible was the sight, <ns0:hi>that</ns0:hi> Moses said, <ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#PDCC" extent="1 letter">
                     <ns0:desc>•</ns0:desc>
                  </ns0:gap> exceedingly fear and quake.</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="22">22 But <ns0:note n="h" place="bottom">The Spirit now adds the Privilege of Christians in the better state, to which they have access by the Gospel-Dis<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />pensation from this 22d, to the 25th Verse; ye have left those Hinderances and Disadvantages instanced in before, but are come to these Helps for your furtherance in Holiness; ye have an Access to all those most excellent, thou invisible things, by Faith, and by it attain them, and are incorpo<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />rated into them, as they follow.</ns0:note> ye are come unto <ns0:note n="i" place="bottom">This is not literally to be understood for the <ns0:hi>Mount,</ns0:hi> on which the City of <ns0:hi>David</ns0:hi> was built, for that was as visible, and touchable as Mount <ns0:hi>Sinai,</ns0:hi> to which it is opposed; but that <ns0:hi>Mount</ns0:hi> which is higher than the highest, as high as Heaven it self, <ns0:hi>v.</ns0:hi> 25. <ns0:hi>ch.</ns0:hi> 9.24. <ns0:hi>Io<ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#PDCC" extent="1 letter">
                           <ns0:desc>•</ns0:desc>
                        </ns0:gap>.</ns0:hi> 3.13. Where is the most orderly Govern<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ment of God for Holiness, <ns0:hi>Mich.</ns0:hi> 4.7. whence all good Gifts, and Gospel-Blessings are conveyed to the Church, of which these Believers were Members, <ns0:hi>Isa.</ns0:hi> 8.18. and 28.16. and 59.20. <ns0:hi>Rev.</ns0:hi> 14.1.</ns0:note> mount Sion, and <ns0:note n="k" place="bottom">Of which the <ns0:hi>living God</ns0:hi> is the Builder and Maker, and wherein he dwelleth, where no<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />thing but Life is, and whence Christ's Voice giveth Life to dead Souls, inabling them to live a Life of Holiness to God, as <ns0:hi>Psalm</ns0:hi> 46.4, 5. and 48.1, 8. and 87.3. <ns0:hi>Isa.</ns0:hi> 60.14. <ns0:hi>Io<ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#PDCC" extent="1 letter">
                           <ns0:desc>•</ns0:desc>
                        </ns0:gap>.</ns0:hi> 5.25. to distinguish this from any earthly City or Corporation, it is said to be the <ns0:hi>Heavenly Ierusalem,</ns0:hi> its Original, Nature and End being all heavenly; a fruitful place, whence Believers are made Partakers of the most spiritual Influences for Holiness; where there is nothing carnal, terrible, deadly, barren, but all causal and productive of Holiness issueth thence, <ns0:hi>Isa.</ns0:hi> 62. and 65.17, 18, 19. and 66.10. <ns0:hi>Iohn</ns0:hi> 17.24. <ns0:hi>Gal.</ns0:hi> 4.26. <ns0:hi>Rev.</ns0:hi> 3.12. and 21.2, 10.</ns0:note> unto the City of the living God, the hea<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />venly Jerusalem, and to <ns0:note n="l" place="bottom">In which City are many excellent Inhabitants with which Believers are in<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />corporated, and to whom they have Relation, as <ns0:hi>Myriads of Angels,</ns0:hi> who are ministring Spirits under the Gospel, as under the Law, full of Holiness, Power, Agility and Indow<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ments fit for their Work, and End; who, tho for number, are thousands and millions of them, <ns0:hi>Psalm</ns0:hi> 68.17. and 103.20. and 104.4. <ns0:hi>Acts</ns0:hi> 7.53. <ns0:hi>Gal.</ns0:hi> 3.19. <ns0:hi>Rev.</ns0:hi> 5.11. yet are all fulfilling their Lord's Pleasure in every place, as ordered by him. Their Ministration of the Law was terrible in fla<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ming Fire, but of the Gospel, most sweet and gracious, <ns0:hi>Luke</ns0:hi> 2.13, 14. At <ns0:hi>Sinai</ns0:hi> they ministred externally, and sensibly, affecting Senses; but from <ns0:hi>Sion</ns0:hi> they minister spiritually, to Hearts, <ns0:hi>Matth.</ns0:hi> 4.11. <ns0:hi>Luke</ns0:hi> 22.43. <ns0:hi>Psalm</ns0:hi> 91.11. resisting evil Spirits ministring wickedly. Their former Ministration tem<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />porary and ceasing, but this everlasting, till they bring all their Trust into <ns0:hi>Abraham</ns0:hi>'s Bosom, <ns0:hi>Luke</ns0:hi> 16.22. And the neglect of this means to help our pursuing Holiness, will God require, <ns0:hi>Heb.</ns0:hi> 2.2.</ns0:note> an innumerable com<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />pany of angels.</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="23">23 To <ns0:note n="m" place="bottom">Other Inhabitants of this heavenly City and Poli<ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#PDCC" extent="1 letter">
                        <ns0:desc>•</ns0:desc>
                     </ns0:gap>y with whom Believers are incorporated, are such, into whose Communion they have admittance here below, <ns0:hi>viz. to the Catholick Assembly of Christ,</ns0:hi> his whole Body, the Fulness of him who filleth all in all; an <ns0:hi>Assembly</ns0:hi> gathered out of <ns0:hi>all</ns0:hi> Nations, <ns0:hi>Rev.</ns0:hi> 5.9. and 7.9. throughout the World, exten<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ded to all Times and Ages, especially to that part of it which is on Earth, sojourning here, fitting for Heaven; the other part is triumphing in it. They are not called, or in<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />corporated only into a particular national Assembly, a straitned Society, as the Old-Testament-Church was, the ge<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />neral Assembly of Saints are more helpful to Holiness, than a lesser, <ns0:hi>Psalm</ns0:hi> 22.27, 28. <ns0:hi>Gal.</ns0:hi> 4.25, 26, 27.</ns0:note> the general assembly and church <ns0:note n="n" place="bottom">This Gene<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ral Assembly is not a Rout, but <ns0:hi>a Church,</ns0:hi> such as are called out of the World with a holy Calling, subjecting themselves to Christ as their Head, and are, as quickned, so ordered and ruled by him: It is not a weak, or an <ns0:hi>Infant-Church,</ns0:hi> but strong and perfect, come unto <ns0:hi>maturity,</ns0:hi> in respect of the great Discoveries of the Mysteries of God, made by Christ to them, <ns0:hi>chap.</ns0:hi> 5.12, 13. and 6.1. <ns0:hi>Gal.</ns0:hi> 4.1, 3, 4. This chosen, called, and well-ordered Society, were only of such Persons, who were the <ns0:hi>First-born of God,</ns0:hi> and Partners of Christ's Sonship and Primogeniture, being regenerated by him, and dignified with his Birth-right-priviledges, <ns0:hi>Rom.</ns0:hi> 8.17, 29.                   </ns0:note> written in hea<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ven, and to <ns0:note n="p" place="bottom">They were as Christians priviledged with an access, not as <ns0:hi>Israel</ns0:hi> had at <ns0:hi>Sinai</ns0:hi> with Fear and Terror, and Trembling, so as to fly from the great Author, Lord and Judge of the Covenant, lest they died, as <ns0:hi>Exod.</ns0:hi> 20.18. but with Liberty and Boldness of Faith, in the strength of Love and with firmness of Hope they come now in <ns0:hi>Sion, Isa.</ns0:hi> 59.20. <ns0:hi>Heb.</ns0:hi> 10.19. unto <ns0:hi>God</ns0:hi> in his Being and Sovereignty, who ruleth all, and who gi<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />veth to all according to their works, and in a most emi<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />nent manner ruleth them, who as he is <ns0:hi>their Iudge,</ns0:hi> hath not as at <ns0:hi>Sinai</ns0:hi> any Barrs to keep them from him, <ns0:hi>Exod.</ns0:hi> 19.12. <ns0:hi>Ephes.</ns0:hi> 2.18. nor is Terrifying and Consuming, as then, <ns0:hi>Deut.</ns0:hi> 5.24, 25. but Justifying them; full of Grace and Love to all approaching him in Christ; his Throne is a Throne of Grace to them, he comforting and encouraging them to make home to him, <ns0:hi>Iohn</ns0:hi> 5.22. <ns0:hi>Acts</ns0:hi> 10.22. <ns0:hi>Rom.</ns0:hi> 3.6. He rewards them gloriously, 2 <ns0:hi>Tim.</ns0:hi> 2.8.                   <ns0:pb facs="tcp:64193:569" />24 And to <ns0:note n="r" place="bottom">The Mediator of the <ns0:hi>Sion</ns0:hi>-Covenant is better than the Mediator at <ns0:hi>Sinai,</ns0:hi> and more able to promote the Holiness required by it. Believers have not now access unto, or de<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />pendance on a <ns0:hi>Moses,</ns0:hi> a meer Man, and a Servant, decla<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ring God's Will, only a Sinner himself, trembling in his Of<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />fice, and weary of his Clients, and whose Ministry is vanish<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ing, as his Person dying; but unto <ns0:hi>God the Son himself incar<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />nate,</ns0:hi> a Son-Mediator, making Sons, and bringing them near<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />er to God, satisfying the Law for them, and writing it on their hearts; above all Sin himself, though a Sacrifice for it, who is able to save to the uttermost, for that he ever liveth to interceed for them, <ns0:hi>chap.</ns0:hi> 1.1, 2, 3. and 3.6. and 7.26. <ns0:hi>Rev.</ns0:hi> 1.13. He is the <ns0:hi>Mediator,</ns0:hi> not of a literal, dark, terrible, charging and condemning, temporary and vanish<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ing Covenant, but of the most spiritual, lightsom, gracious, justifying, sanctifying and everlasting Testamental-Dispensa<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />tion of God, more effectually influencing Souls to Holiness than the Old, <ns0:hi>chap.</ns0:hi> 8.10, 11. 2 <ns0:hi>Cor.</ns0:hi> 3.6. and 5.19.</ns0:note> 
                  <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">Chap. 9.14.</ns0:note> Jesus the Mediator of the new <ns0:note n="‖" place="margin">Or, <ns0:hi>Testament.</ns0:hi>
                  </ns0:note> covenant, and <ns0:note n="s" place="bottom">
                     <ns0:hi>The Sacrifice</ns0:hi> ratifying the <ns0:hi>Sion</ns0:hi>-Covenant is unexpressibly better than all the Typical Sacrifices confirming that at <ns0:hi>Sinai,</ns0:hi> it eminently purchasing and securing Holiness to those inte<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />rested in it. <ns0:hi>The Blood of the immaculate Lamb of God, sprinkled</ns0:hi> on penitent, believing Sinners, which hath purchased Par<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />don for them, and as follows, the Spirit to sanctify them throughout, and perfect Holiness in them, <ns0:hi>chap.</ns0:hi> 9. 12. 1 <ns0:hi>Peter</ns0:hi> 1.18. 1 Iohn 1.7, 9. and so are freed from access to the sprinkling of the Blood of Sacrificed Beasts, which was only typical and weak to purge the Conscience, calling Sin to remembrance yearly and daily, which was now forbidden and rejected as of no worth, and which, like <ns0:hi>Abel</ns0:hi>'s crieth for Revenge and Condemnation, <ns0:hi>Gen.</ns0:hi> 4.10. Since <ns0:hi>their Blood</ns0:hi> now offered when Christ had spilt his, was accounted of God as the Blood of Innocents slain, as <ns0:hi>Isa.</ns0:hi> 66.3. Others render the <ns0:hi>Blood of</ns0:hi> Abel <ns0:hi>for the Blood of sprinkling of the Sacrifice that</ns0:hi> Abel <ns0:hi>offered unto God,</ns0:hi> Gen. 4.4. which was sprinkled upon him; and so prefer Christ's Sacrifice, not only to the Mosaical Sacrifices, but to all that have been from the beginning of the World, which though accepted by God, yet not like Christ, of which they were the Types. The summ of all these comparisons, is to shew the greater helps, motives and encouragements that Chri<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />stians have to pursue and perfect Holiness than all the Old-Testament-Church had before them.</ns0:note> to <ns0:note n="†" place="margin">Exod. 24.8. 1 Pet. 1.2.</ns0:note> the blood of sprink<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ling, that speaketh better things than <ns0:hi>that of</ns0:hi> Abel.</ns0:p>

There remaining no more Sacrifice for such Sin and Sinners.</ns0:note> much more <ns0:hi>shall not</ns0:hi> we <ns0:hi>escape,</ns0:hi> if we turn away from him that <ns0:hi>speaketh</ns0:hi> from heaven:</ns0:p>

                  <ns0:pb facs="tcp:64193:570" />28 Wherefore <ns0:note n="a" place="bottom">In his Verse the Apostle follows his Doctrine with Counsel to several Duties, such as concern the first Table, and terminate on God in this 28 and 29 Verse; such as concern the second Table, <ns0:hi>chap.</ns0:hi> 13.1, &c.                <ns0:p n="29">29 For <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">Deut. 9.3.</ns0:note> our God <ns0:hi>is</ns0:hi> a consuming fire <ns0:note n="c" place="bottom">The motive inforcing this Duty, is no less terrible than that given to <ns0:hi>Israel</ns0:hi> under the Law, obliging their o<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />bedience to that Covenant-Dispensation, <ns0:hi>Deut.</ns0:hi> 4.23, 24. <ns0:hi>The Lord thy God is a consuming Fire, even a Iealous God.</ns0:hi> He that was so respecting the Transgression of the Legal, will much more be so as to this Gospel-Covenant. <ns0:hi>God Almighty</ns0:hi> the most Gracious, and yet the most Just Being, their own God by Covenant-obtestation; yet will be to them if they break his Covenant, and do not, through Christ, acceptably serve him with reverence and godly fear, as <ns0:hi>Fire consuming them.</ns0:hi> His Gospel-Law in the contempt of it, will be as the Fiery Law at <ns0:hi>Sinai,</ns0:hi> adjudging such Sinners unto Fire un<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />quenchable, <ns0:hi>ch.</ns0:hi> 10.27, to 32. comp. <ns0:hi>Matth.</ns0:hi> 3.12. and 25.41. 2 <ns0:hi>Thess.</ns0:hi> 1.7, 8, 9.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
